title: The Coaster Queue
covers: how to solve a one-step inequality with inverse operations, graph its whole solution set, and test values to see that it has many solutions, not just one
cert: solving one-step inequalities and graphing the whole solution set

intro.caption: Lesson 8-6 — solving and graphing inequalities. Screamline Park has a brand-new coaster, the Thunder Twist. It cannot open until the queue rules are set. Three gates and a boss lock stand in the way.

balloons.t: The Thunder Twist opens when every queue rule is solved, graphed and tested. Rules are rules.
Race you, Rafi. Most rules solved wins.
Long queue. Bored people. Unguarded funnel cake. I love this ride already.
12 people are in line. The line holds up to 40. So I let in exactly 28 more. Done!
Exactly 28? What if only 10 more show up? Is that against the rules?

pages.caption: Gus found ONE number. But "up to 40" is an inequality. It has a whole solution set: 28 works, and so do 10, 3 and 0.

balloons.t: x is how many more we let in. Undo the + 12 on both sides.
The stand started with f funnel cakes. Bandit took 5. More than 15 are left. So f − 5 > 15.
I took 5. Allegedly. Solve it before I take a sixth.
A coaster run needs at least 25 riders. 9 are buckled in. So r + 9 ≥ 25.
Don't trust it. Test it. Put numbers in and see what's true.
Last rule: x − 8 < 30. Solve, graph, test.
Hey, panel. We got this. Please be nice.

win.caption: Solve an inequality like an equation: undo the operation on both sides. The answer is a solution set, not one number. Graph it with a circle and a ray, then test a value to check.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Solve the Line Rule
gates.badge: Line Boss — Solve with Inverse Operations
gates.prompt: The queue has 12 people. It can hold no more than 40. Solve x + 12 ≤ 40 for the number of people x you can still let in.
hints: Conceptual: solving an inequality works like solving an equation. Do the inverse operation to both sides and keep the same symbol.
Procedural: the inverse of adding 12 is subtracting 12. Subtract it from both sides, then read what x can be.

steps: Subtract 7 from both sides: y + 7 − 7 ≤ 20 − 7, so y ≤ 13.
That is a solution set: 13 works, and so do 10, 5 and 0.

items.label: x + 12 ≤ 40, so x ≤
items.aria: the number x is less than or equal to

fb.msg: 52 is 40 + 12. You added. Undo + 12 by subtracting 12 from both sides.
40 is the limit for the whole line. 12 people are already in it, so subtract 12.

items.fbDefault: Subtract 12 from both sides of x + 12 ≤ 40.

items.q: Gus wrote x = 28 on the queue sign. Which sign is right?

options.fb: That is Gus's mistake. 28 is only one solution. Letting in 10 people also keeps the line at 40 or less.

options.t: x ≥ 28: let in 28 people or more
options.fb: That flips the rule. Letting in 30 people makes 42 in line, and 42 ≤ 40 is false.

options.t: x ≤ 28: let in 28 people or fewer
x ≤ 52: let in 52 people or fewer
options.fb: 52 comes from adding 12. Letting in 52 people makes 64 in line. Too many!

gates.pass: Hana writes x ≤ 28 on the sign. Gus crosses out his "exactly." Hana: "One rule for me."

gates.title: Gate 2 · Graph the Funnel Cakes
gates.prompt: The stand started with f funnel cakes. Bandit took 5, and more than 15 are left: f − 5 > 15. Solve it, then graph the solution set.
hints: Conceptual: the solution set is every number the stand could have started with. The symbol you start with is the symbol you graph.
Procedural: the inverse of subtracting 5 is adding 5. Do it to both sides. Then pick the circle and the direction.

steps: Practice rule: k − 6 > 2. Add 6 to both sides: k > 8.
> does not include 8, so draw an open circle at 8.
Greater than means the ray points right.
worked.a: p ≥ 12: closed circle at 12, ray right

items.label: f − 5 > 15, so f >
items.aria: the number f is greater than

fb.msg: 10 is 15 − 5. Undo − 5 by ADDING 5 to both sides.
15 is how many are left. The stand started with more, because Bandit took 5.

items.fbDefault: Add 5 to both sides of f − 5 > 15.

fb.msg: 10 is 15 − 5. Solve first: f > 20, so the boundary point is 20.
22 is a solution, but the graph starts at the boundary point, 20.

items.fbDefault: Solve first. The boundary point is the number in f > ___.
items.fbOpen: > does not include 20. If the stand had exactly 20, then 15 would be left, and 15 > 15 is false. Open circle.
items.fbClosed: This boundary is included, so fill the circle.
items.fbDir: f > 20 means MORE than 20. Bigger numbers are to the right.

gates.pass: Odalys prints it: "Stand started with more than 20 cakes." Bandit: "No comment."

gates.title: Gate 3 · Test the Riders
gates.prompt: A coaster run needs at least 25 riders, and 9 are buckled in: r + 9 ≥ 25, so r ≥ 16. Test values to see which ones work.
hints: Conceptual: a value is a solution if it makes the inequality a true statement. An inequality can have many solutions.
Procedural: substitute the value for r in r + 9 ≥ 25. Add, then ask: is the result 25 or more?

steps: Test 5: 5 + 2 = 7, and 7 > 6 is true. So 5 is a solution.
Test 4: 4 + 2 = 6, and 6 > 6 is false. So 4 is not.

items.q: Which values of r make r + 9 ≥ 25 true? Pick all.

options.fb: 15 + 9 = 24, and 24 ≥ 25 is false. One rider short!
9 is a number in the rule, not a solution. 9 + 9 = 18, and 18 ≥ 25 is false.

items.fbMiss: Another value works too. An inequality can have more than one solution.
items.fbExtra: One pick makes a false statement. Substitute it and add 9.

items.q: How many numbers are in the solution set of r ≥ 16?

options.fb: 16 is the boundary point, not the only solution. 17, 20 and 30 all make r ≥ 16 true too.

options.t: Infinitely many: 16 and every number above it
None, because 16 + 9 is not more than 25
options.fb: 16 + 9 = 25, and 25 ≥ 25 is true. The line under ≥ means 25 counts.

gates.pass: 16 riders, 30 riders, 100 riders: all of them work. Rafi: "That ties it. One rule each."

gates.title: Boss Gate · The Launch Lock
gates.prompt: The launch panel shows x − 8 < 30. Solve it, graph it, and test the boundary.
hints: Conceptual: undo the operation on both sides and keep the symbol. The answer is a range of numbers, so graph all of it.
Procedural: add 8 to both sides. Then choose open or closed for <, and the direction for "less than".

steps: Practice rule: w − 11 ≥ 4. Add 11 to both sides: w ≥ 15.
Graph: closed circle at 15, ray to the right.
Test 15: 15 − 11 = 4, and 4 ≥ 4 is true. It checks.

items.label: Lock 1 · x − 8 < 30, so x <
items.aria: the number x is less than

fb.msg: 22 is 30 − 8. Undo − 8 by ADDING 8 to both sides.
30 is the right side before solving. Add 8 to both sides first.

items.fbDefault: Add 8 to both sides of x − 8 < 30.

fb.msg: 30 is the right side before solving. The solution is x < 38, so the boundary point is 38.
36 is a solution, but the graph starts at the boundary point, 38.

items.fbDefault: The boundary point is the number in x < ___.
items.fbOpen: < does not include 38. Test it: 38 − 8 = 30, and 30 < 30 is false. Open circle.
items.fbClosed: This boundary is included, so fill the circle.
items.fbDir: x < 38 means LESS than 38. Smaller numbers are to the left.

items.q: Lock 3 · Gus says x = 38 must work, because 38 is "the answer." Is 38 a solution of x − 8 < 30?

options.fb: 38 is the boundary point, not "the answer." Substitute it: 38 − 8 = 30, and 30 < 30 is false.
38 − 8 does equal 30. But the rule is LESS than 30, and 30 is not less than 30.

gates.pass: The screen glows green. Mr. Krank nods once. "The Thunder Twist is open."

journal.heading: Lesson 8-6 — what the coaster queue taught us
rows: Undo the operation on both sides. x + 12 ≤ 40 becomes x ≤ 28. f − 5 > 15 becomes f > 20.
x ≤ 28 means 28, 20, 10 and 0 all work. Gus's "exactly 28" missed most of the solution set.
Circle at the boundary point: open for < and >, closed for ≤ and ≥. Ray right for greater, left for less.
Substitute a value. 16 + 9 = 25 and 25 ≥ 25 is true. 38 − 8 = 30 and 30 < 30 is false.
journal.quote: "An inequality is like funnel cake. There is never just one." — Bandit

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 8-6 (Solve and Graph Inequalities) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. It covers only this lesson: solving one-step inequalities with addition and subtraction, graphing the solution set, and testing values to show an inequality has many solutions.
standards: Understand solving an equation or inequality as a process of answering which values make it true; use substitution to determine whether a given number makes an equation or inequality true
